title: Cancer Screenings Worth Knowing
hook: Screening looks for cancer before symptoms start — and for a few common cancers, that early catch dramatically improves the odds.
key_points: Screening tests check for cancer in people without symptoms, when treatment works best.
Strong evidence backs screening for breast, cervical, colorectal, and lung cancers.
Recommended ages and intervals depend on your age, sex, and risk factors.
Your provider can tailor a screening schedule to your personal and family history.
content_html: Cancer is far more treatable when it's caught early — and for several common cancers, we have reliable tests that find it before any symptoms appear. The trick is knowing which screenings apply to you, and when.
extra_html: The CDC explains that screening means checking for cancer in people who have no symptoms, with the goal of catching it — or pre-cancerous changes — at the most treatable stage. The strongest evidence supports a handful: mammograms for breast cancer, Pap and HPV tests for cervical cancer, colonoscopy or stool-based tests for colorectal cancer, and low-dose CT scans for lung cancer in people with a heavy smoking history. The recommended starting age and how often to repeat each test depend on your age, sex, and risk factors, and guidelines are periodically updated as evidence evolves. Because the right schedule is personal — shaped by family history and individual risk — the practical move is to ask your provider which screenings you're due for rather than guess.

source.name: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

related.title: Why Regular Checkups Matter
related.hook: The whole point of a checkup is to catch trouble while it's still quiet — before symptoms show up and while it's easiest to treat.

related.title: The First New Sunscreen Filter in the U.S. in 20 Years
related.hook: The FDA approved bemotrizinol — a broad-spectrum UV filter used for decades in Europe and Asia — the first new sunscreen ingredient cleared in the U.S. in about 20 years.

related.title: One Blood Test for Many Cancers?
related.hook: A single blood draw that screens for many cancers at once could win FDA approval within months — a potential shift in how cancer gets caught early.

related.title: The Colon Cancer Warning Signs Young Adults Shrug Off
related.hook: Colorectal cancer is now the leading cause of cancer death in people under 50 — and it's still rising. A handful of symptoms are worth taking seriously long before the recommended screening age.

flashcards.prompt: What is the point of a cancer screening test?
flashcards.back_html: To find cancer (or pre-cancerous changes) in people without symptoms — catching it early, when treatment is most likely to succeed.

flashcards.prompt: For which cancers is routine screening strongly recommended for the general population?

choices.text: Every type of cancer that exists

flashcards.explanation_html: The CDC notes strong evidence supports screening for breast, cervical, colorectal, and (for those at high risk) lung cancers; recommendations vary by age and risk.
